content: Symmetry generally conveys two primary meanings. The first meaning refers to an imprecise sense of harmonious or aesthetically pleasing proportionality and balance, which reflects beauty or perfection. The second meaning is a precise and well-defined concept of balance or patterned self-similarity that can be demonstrated or proven according to the rules of a formal system, such as through geometry, physics, or other disciplines. Although these meanings are distinct, in some contexts, both interpretations of symmetry are related and discussed in parallel. For instance, symmetry may be observed in relation to the passage of time, as a spatial relationship, through geometric transformations such as scaling, reflection, and rotation, through other kinds of functional transformations, or as an aspect of abstract objects, theoretical models, language, music, and even knowledge itself. This article describes these notions of symmetry from three perspectives. The first perspective is mathematical, where symmetries are defined and categorized with precision. The second perspective relates symmetry to science and technology, where symmetries underpin some of the most profound results of modern physics, including aspects of space and time. Finally, the third perspective explores symmetry in the humanities, encompassing its rich and varied use in history, architecture, art, and religion. The opposite of symmetry is asymmetry. In mathematics, an object is said to be symmetric with respect to a given mathematical operation if, when the operation is applied, the object or its appearance remains unchanged. Two objects are symmetric to each other with respect to a given group of operations if one can be obtained from the other by some of the operations, and vice versa. Symmetries are also found in living organisms, including humans and other animals. In two-dimensional geometry, the main types of symmetry of interest are those related to basic Euclidean plane isometries: translations, rotations, reflections, and glide reflections. The set of all symmetry operations considered on all objects in a set X can be modeled as a group action, where the symmetry group of an object consists of all operations that leave the object unchanged. If the symmetry group of an object is the trivial group, the object is said to be asymmetric; otherwise, it is symmetric. For example, a group of bijections of a space induces a group action on objects within it. The symmetry group of an object consists of all operations that leave the object invariant. Some subgroups of the symmetry group of the space may not correspond to the symmetry group of any object. For instance, in one-dimensional space, the group of all translations implies that any pattern invariant under translation is also invariant under reflection. In the context of vector fields, symmetry operations may involve transformations that rotate or invert vectors and pseudovectors according to specific rules. For example, a cylinder with a current perpendicular to its axis exhibits cylindrical symmetry without mirror planes through the axis. Similarly, a rotating cylinder demonstrates angular momentum and velocity symmetries. Symmetry groups can act transitively on repeated features of an object, meaning that for every pair of occurrences of the feature, there exists a symmetry operation mapping one to the other. For example, in one-dimensional space, certain sets of points may exhibit transitive symmetry, while others do not. Non-isometric symmetries involve transformations beyond Euclidean isometries, such as similarity transformations, affine transformations, or inversive geometry. Examples include dilations, oblique reflection symmetry, and circle inversions. Reflection symmetry, also known as mirror symmetry or bilateral symmetry, occurs when an object is indistinguishable from its reflected image. In one-dimensional space, this involves a point of symmetry; in two dimensions, an axis of symmetry; and in three dimensions, a plane of symmetry. For example, a square has four axes of symmetry, while a circle has infinitely many. Reflection symmetry is also observed in biological organisms, such as the bilateral symmetry of humans. Rotational symmetry refers to symmetry with respect to rotations in Euclidean space. The symmetry group of rotational symmetry is a subgroup of the group of direct isometries. For example, the laws of physics are invariant under the special orthogonal group SO(3), which corresponds to rotational symmetry in three-dimensional space. According to Noether's theorem, rotational symmetry in a physical system is equivalent to the conservation of angular momentum. Translational symmetry leaves an object invariant under a group of translations, either discrete or continuous. Glide reflection symmetry combines reflection in a line or plane with translation along that line or plane, resulting in the same object. Rotoreflection symmetry involves rotation about an axis combined with reflection in a plane perpendicular to that axis. Helical symmetry is observed in objects such as springs, drill bits, and augers. It combines rotational symmetry with translational symmetry along the axis of rotation. Infinite helical symmetry occurs when an object appears identical after any small rotation and corresponding translation along its axis. DNA is an example of non-repeating helical symmetry. Scale symmetry refers to the property of an object remaining unchanged when expanded or reduced in size. While scale symmetry is rare in physical systems, it is demonstrated by fractals, which exhibit self-similarity at different levels of magnification. Fractals, such as the Mandelbrot set, are used in computer-generated imagery to create realistic virtual worlds. In physics, symmetry has been generalized to mean invariance under transformations, making it a powerful tool in theoretical physics. Symmetries underlie the laws of nature and determine the properties of particles. For example, Noether's theorem links continuous symmetries to conserved quantities, while Wigner's classification relates symmetries to particle properties. In classical physics, symmetry in everyday objects is often an approximation rather than an exact mathematical property. For instance, a precisely machined triangle may appear symmetric under rotation, but detailed examination reveals unique features at each corner. In contrast, quantum physics deals with objects where symmetry assertions become experimentally precise, such as electrons and atoms. In this realm, symmetry plays a fundamental role in the behavior of particles and the laws governing them. The transition from approximate to exact symmetries highlights the deep connection between symmetry and quantum mechanics. When physical systems exhibit exact symmetries, their mathematical descriptions become precise definitions of their underlying nature. This interplay between symmetry and quantum mechanics underscores the importance of symmetry as a unifying principle in science and mathematics.
